subject: korean
title: Who really bought the cake?
goal: Weigh several relayed statements, work out who each report points to, and decide which claim the evidence supports best.
thinking: Inferring the original words from a report
Explaining how sure you are and why
differsFromPlain: Plain practice turns one direct sentence into a report. Here three reports disagree and you decide which one to trust, using who is speaking about whom.
prerequisites: Can read short Korean sentences with polite endings
Has seen sentences of the type 'someone said that ...' in class
material:
Your class bought a birthday cake for the teacher, and 은서 asked three classmates who paid. These are 은서's notes, in her own words:

1) 민호는 자기가 케이크를 샀대요.
2) 수빈이는 민호가 케이크를 샀다고 했어요.
3) 지후는 수빈이가 케이크를 샀대요.

Note: 자기 here points back to the person who is the subject of the sentence.

steps.prompt: In note 1, what did 민호 most likely say to 은서 himself?

options.reveals: A speaker rarely names himself in the third person; 자기 in the note points back to the speaker.
You read 자기 as a pointer back to the speaker, so he spoke about himself.
That names a different person; check who 자기 points to in the note.
A negative sentence would be reported with 안 샀대요; the note has no negation.

steps.explain: 자기 refers back to 민호, the subject. When he talks about himself he would say 제가/내가 (I), and the report changes it to 자기.
hints: Ask yourself who the subject of note 1 is, and whom 자기 points to.
Imagine you are 민호 speaking directly: which word would you use for yourself?

steps.prompt: Using all three notes, who most likely bought the cake?

options.reveals: This rests on one report (note 3) that the other two notes do not support.
지후 appears only as a reporter; no note says he bought it.
You looked for the answer that the most notes, including the person's own statement, support.
Some answers are better supported than others even when you are not 100% sure.

steps.explain: Note 1 is 민호's own claim and note 2 repeats it. Only note 3 names 수빈. The best-supported answer is 민호, although more information could still change it.
hints: Count how many notes point to each person.
Does any note come straight from the person it names?

steps.prompt: In English or Korean, explain your choice in 2-3 sentences. What evidence did you use, and what would make you less sure?
selfAssess: Did I use the person's own statement as evidence?
Did I say how many notes support my answer?
Did I name something that would change my mind?

modelAnswers.text: Probably 민호. He says he did it himself (자기), and 수빈 says the same thing, so two reports agree. Only 지후 names 수빈, so that one conflicts. I would be less sure if 수빈 only heard it from 민호, because then it is not a separate source.
민호예요. 민호 자기가 샀다고 했고 수빈이도 같은 말을 했어요. 지후만 달라요. I would ask 지후 how he knows.

badAnswers.text: I think 민호 because he is nice.
badAnswers.why: No evidence from the notes.
No reasoning and does not use the notes.

steps.humanReview: Whether the student separates first-hand from second-hand evidence and states what could change the answer.
hints: Mention which notes agree and which one does not.
Say whose own words (first-hand) you have and whose you only have second-hand.

rubric.full: Uses at least two notes, separates 민호's own words from reports about him
rubric.partial: Names the answer but uses only one note

rubric.full: Says what could change the answer (e.g. 수빈 only heard it from 민호)
rubric.none: Claims certainty or says nothing can be known

alternatives: Answering '민호' with the reasoning that the person himself and a second person agree is the expected line.
A student who says 'ask 수빈 and 지후 how they know' before deciding is also reasoning well.
hardCases: If 수빈 only heard it from 민호, notes 1 and 2 are not independent; some students notice this.

cautions.language: -대요 and -다고 했어요 are two forms of the same kind of report. 자기 refers back to the sentence subject; it is not the same as 'friend'.
cautions.culture: Birthday gifts for teachers vary; the setting is only a neutral class scene and none of the names are real people.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The notes are plain text, numbered 1 to 3.

auto: The choice items (key: step 1 b, step 2 c) and the surface checks of the explanation
human: Quality of the explanation and whether the confidence is justified

subject: korean
title: Whose 'me' is it?
goal: Find the report that points to the wrong person, repair it, and state the general idea behind the repair.
thinking: Checking each reported line against the original
Re-pointing words such as 나 to the new speaker's situation
differsFromPlain: Plain practice changes endings (-해요 to -한대요). Here every ending is right and the error hides in who a word points to.
prerequisites: Can read short Korean messages with polite endings
Has seen 'someone told me ...' sentences in class
material:
오빠 left a voice message for his younger sister 지아:

'지아야, 엄마한테 전해 줘. 오늘 나 늦게 가. 저녁은 먼저 드시라고 해. 그리고 나한테는 전화하지 말라고 해. 내일은 일찍 나가.'

지아 now tells 엄마 (polite style):

steps.prompt: One of 지아's sentences points to the wrong person. Which line?
steps.explain: Line 3 is wrong. In 오빠's message 나한테는 means 오빠, but 지아 is the one speaking now, so 저한테는 would mean 지아. Lines 1, 2 and 4 keep the meaning and use fitting endings.
hints: Take one line at a time and put it back into 오빠's words.
Look for words that mean 'me' or 'you' and ask who the speaker is each time.

steps.prompt: Write line 3 again so that it is correct. Keep the polite style.

checks.label: does not use 저/나 for the wrong person
reports a request not to call

selfAssess: Does my sentence say who should not be called?
Would 엄마 understand it as a message from 오빠?

modelAnswers.text: 그리고 오빠한테는 전화하지 말래요.
그리고 자기한테는 전화하지 말라고 했어요.

badAnswers.why: Still points to 지아.
Not a report; sounds like an order from 지아 to 엄마.

steps.humanReview: Natural wording and whether 자기 is used correctly; a plain 오빠 is the safest.
hints: Ask who 오빠 means by 나한테는, and who 지아 should name instead.
Keep the ending that reports a request not to do something.

steps.prompt: Which idea explains the repair best?

options.text: The ending is the only part that changes when you pass a message on.
options.reveals: Here the endings were right and the meaning still broke.

options.text: Only formal messages need changes of words.
options.reveals: Even a casual message from a sibling needs the same care.

options.text: Words such as 나 and 너 must be re-aimed at the people in the new situation.
options.reveals: You noticed that words pointing at people shift with the speaker.

steps.explain: Words that point at the speaker or listener (나, 너, 우리) change when the speaker changes. Endings alone are not enough.
hints: Compare the original word with the repaired word: what stayed the same, what changed?
Think of what would happen if 엄마 passed it on again.

rubric.full: Picks line 3 and can say which word is wrong and why
rubric.partial: Picks a line with a reason that is only about endings

rubric.full: Names 오빠 or 자기 and keeps a reported ending
rubric.partial: Changes the word but loses the reported ending

alternatives: 자기한테는 is also a good repair if the student knows how 자기 points back.
오빠 can be replaced by the child's own name for the brother in other families (형 for a male speaker).
hardCases: A student who writes 오빠한테는 전화하지 말라고 하셨어요 uses honorific 하셨 for a sibling; polite but not needed.

cautions.language: Reported speech: 나 (I) becomes the person's name, 자기 or 오빠. The endings -래요/-대요 are written as one word, no space.
cautions.culture: 오빠 is what a younger sister calls her older brother; younger brothers say 형. Family terms depend on who speaks.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Lines are numbered by the page from 1. Read 'the ending -래요' aloud as 'rae-yo'.

auto: The line chosen in step 1, the surface checks of the repair, step 3
human: Natural wording of the repaired sentence

subject: korean
title: A family dinner built from four messages
goal: Read messages that were passed on from person to person, turn them into exact limits, and find several plans that keep all of them.
thinking: Turning reported wording into limits (before, until, at most)
differsFromPlain: Plain practice asks for one time in one sentence. Here four relayed messages give limits that must all hold together.
prerequisites: Can read times such as 7시 and 9시
Has seen 'someone told me ...' sentences in class; 전에, 까지 and 넘게 are explained in the hints
material:
Your family plans dinner for 할머니's birthday. All times are in the evening (오후). Four people passed on messages:

엄마: '아빠가 7시 전에는 못 온대. 아빠가 와야 먹을 수 있어.'
이모: '동생이 9시 전에는 먹기 시작해야 한대. 9시부터 학원에 가거든.'
삼촌: '할머니께서 10시에는 주무신대. 그때까지 식사가 끝나야 해.'
고모: '의사 선생님이 할머니는 천천히 한 시간 이상 드시래. 그렇지만 두 시간 넘게는 앉아 계시지 말래.'

steps.prompt: What does 고모 pass on with '두 시간 넘게는 앉아 계시지 말래'?

options.text: The meal must last longer than 2 hours.
options.reveals: 넘게 means 'beyond'; 말래 reports 'do not'.

options.text: The meal must last exactly 2 hours.
options.reveals: The sentence sets a limit, it does not ask for one exact length.

options.text: The meal may last 2 hours at most.
options.reveals: You combined 넘게 (beyond) with 말래 (do not) correctly.

steps.explain: 넘게 means more than; 하지 말래 reports 'do not'. So the meal may not go beyond 2 hours, and exactly 2 hours is still fine.
hints: Translate 두 시간 넘게 first, then the ending 말래.
Test: would 2 hours exactly break the rule?

steps.prompt: Find 3 different dinner plans that obey all four messages. s = hour when dinner starts, e = hour when dinner ends (whole hours, evening).

constraints.fail: The meal must be at least one hour (고모's message).
The meal may not be longer than two hours (고모's message).

steps.explain: The possible plans are 7-8, 7-9, 8-9 and 8-10. For example 7 to 9 starts after 아빠 arrives, starts before 9, ends before 10 and lasts 2 hours.
hints: Write each message as a small rule: 'not before', 'before', 'by', 'at least', 'at most'.
Pick the start first (which hours are left?), then the end.
Check the length e minus s last.

because.prompt: Tell 아빠 (polite style) your plan: when dinner starts and ends, and one reason from a message you pass on.

checks.label: passes on a reason with a reported form

selfAssess: Do the times in my text match one of my plans?
Is the reason really in one of the four messages?

modelAnswers.text: 저녁은 8시에 시작해서 10시에 끝낼 거예요. 할머니께서 10시에는 주무신대요.
7시에 시작해서 8시에 끝내요. 동생이 9시 전에 먹기 시작해야 한대요.

badAnswers.why: No times and no reason.
No reason passed on.

because.humanReview: Whether the times form a valid plan and the reason matches a real message.
hints: Choose one of your plans, then one of the four messages that limits it.
Use a reporting ending (-대요, -래요, -다고 했어요) for the reason.

rubric.full: Every plan obeys all four messages
Report names the plan and a real reason with a reported form

alternatives: Other lengths (1 or 2 hours) are fine as long as all limits hold.
A student who treats '9시 전에는' as 'up to and including 9' will accept start 9; the explanation shows why not.
hardCases: Is exactly 7시 allowed for 아빠? Yes: '7시 전에는 못 온대' only rules out earlier times.

cautions.language: 전에 = before, -까지 = until, 넘게 = beyond. Times are written with 시. Hours are evening hours, so no 오후 is needed in the build.
cautions.culture: Family birthday dinners at home or a restaurant are widespread; 할머니's birthday dinner is a neutral scene.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Messages are plain lines starting with the sender's name.

auto: Whether each plan satisfies all limits, times and reported ending in the text
human: Whether the reason matches the plan

subject: korean
title: What must I ask before I pass it on?
goal: Decide which missing details a message needs before it can be relayed, then write the finished relay.
differsFromPlain: Plain practice gives you a full message to report. Here the message is incomplete and you decide what to ask first.
prerequisites: Can read short Korean messages with polite endings
Has seen 'someone told me ...' sentences in class
material: In the hallway 하나 says quickly to 지우: '선생님이 준비물 가져오래.' 지우 wants to tell 엄마 tonight so she can prepare it, but 지우 does not know what to bring.

steps.prompt: Which questions must 지우 ask 하나 so that 엄마 can prepare the right thing? Choose all that are needed.

options.text: 하나는 어디에서 들었어요? (Where did you hear it?)
options.reveals: Where 하나 heard it does not change what 엄마 must do.
You saw that '준비물' alone does not say which item.

options.text: 선생님이 웃으면서 말했어요? (Did the teacher smile?)
options.reveals: The teacher's mood does not change what must be prepared.
You noticed that a deadline is part of the task.
You saw that the amount also decides what 엄마 buys.

steps.explain: 엄마 needs to know what, by when and how many. Where 하나 heard it or whether the teacher smiled does not change what to prepare.
hints: Imagine 엄마 goes shopping tonight: what would she not know yet?
Cross out questions whose answer would not change what 엄마 does.

steps.prompt: 하나 answers: '색연필이야. 금요일까지. 12색으로 한 통.' Now tell 엄마 in Korean what 선생님 said (polite style).
selfAssess: Does my message let 엄마 prepare without asking more?
Do I report an instruction (bring it), not a fact?

modelAnswers.text: 선생님이 금요일까지 12색 색연필 한 통을 가져오래요.
선생님이 금요일까지 색연필 한 통을 가져오라고 하셨어요. 12색이래요.
선생님이 금요일까지 12색 색연필 한 통을 가져와야 한대요.

badAnswers.why: Deadline and amount are missing.

badAnswers.text: 선생님이 금요일까지 색연필 한 통을 가져온대요.
badAnswers.why: Reports a statement, not an instruction.

steps.humanReview: Natural wording of the relay and whether it is complete.
hints: Use 선생님이 ... and a reporting ending for an instruction.
Put the item, the deadline and the amount into one or two sentences.

rubric.full: Chooses exactly what, by when and how many
rubric.partial: Chooses two of the three, or adds one irrelevant question

rubric.full: Gives item, deadline, amount and a reported instruction

alternatives: Some students also ask for the colour or brand; that is reasonable but not needed for a relay.
A student who asks '다른 반도 가져와요?' (does other classes bring it too?) is thinking, but 엄마 does not need it.
hardCases: Whether to say 선생님이 ... 하셨어요 (honorific) or ... 래요 depends on how formal the family is.

cautions.language: 가져오래요 comes from 가져오라고 해요 (a reported instruction); 가져온대요 would report a fact, which is a different meaning.
cautions.culture: Bringing art supplies to class is common in Korea; the example is neutral.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The questions are given in Korean plus an English gloss in brackets.

auto: The set of needed questions, presence of item/deadline/amount/instruction form

subject: korean
title: Is 3:00 the deadline or the start?
goal: Revise a judgement about what a relayed message means as new evidence arrives, and rewrite the message so it keeps the lost detail.
thinking: Repairing a message that lost a detail
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reports one sentence once. Here the same message appears in three forms and you update your reading.
prerequisites: Can read times such as 3시
Has seen 'someone told me ...' sentences in class
material: 두리 will go to a special class tomorrow. The information reaches 두리 in pieces. Decide at each step what you believe, then read what comes next.

steps.prompt: Follow the messages and decide at each step when 두리 should arrive.

stages.info: 하나 tells 두리 in the hallway: '선생님이 내일 3시까지 오래.'
stages.ask: When does 두리 need to be there?

options.reveals: 까지 marks a limit, not an exact time.
You read 까지 as 'up to'.
까지 looks backwards from 3:00; after 3:00 would be too late.

stages.after: 까지 sets a latest time: be there by 3:00.

stages.info: 반장 writes to 소희 in the class chat: '수업은 3시에 시작한대.'

options.text: The two messages contradict each other, so ignore the first.
options.reveals: The messages do not contradict: arriving by the start time is possible.

options.text: Class starts at 3:00, so 'by 3:00' might have lost a detail.
options.reveals: You noticed that a short message may not be the whole message.

options.text: Both are clear: arrive at 3:00 and be done.
options.reveals: Reasonable with this information; check what the teacher actually said.

stages.after: Both messages can be true. But 'by 3:00' for a class that starts at 3:00 is odd: why would the teacher say it?

stages.info: 하나 remembers the teacher's exact words: '수업은 3시에 시작하니까 10분 전까지 오세요.'

options.reveals: You used the teacher's original words and not the shortened relay.
That was the shortened relay; the original sets an earlier time.
That reads 10분 as a later time; 전 means before.

stages.after: The relay 3시까지 lost '10분 전'. The original gives a reason (the class starts at 3) and a time (10 minutes before).

steps.reflect: Short relays can drop numbers or reasons. When two messages seem to fit, ask whether the first one is the whole story.
hints: At each stage, write your own answer before you read the options.
If a new message fits the old one, ask whether it adds a detail.

steps.prompt: Write the correct message for 두리's mother (polite style), including the detail that was lost.

checks.label: includes the earlier arrival time (10 minutes, or 2:50)
says it is earlier than 3 (전, 일찍 or 2:50)

selfAssess: Would 두리's mother know to arrive earlier than the class start?
Did I report an instruction and not a fact?

modelAnswers.text: 선생님이 3시 10분 전까지 오래요.
선생님이 수업이 3시에 시작하니까 10분 전까지 오라고 하셨어요.
수업은 3시에 시작하니까 10분 일찍 오라고 하셨어요.
선생님이 2시 50분까지 오래요.

badAnswers.why: Loses the 10 minutes.
Reports a fact about 선생님, not an instruction.

steps.humanReview: Natural wording and whether the reason is kept.
hints: Include both the class start time and the earlier arrival time.
Use a reporting ending for an instruction.

rubric.full: Changes the reading when the exact words arrive and says why
Message keeps the earlier arrival time (10 minutes before 3:00, or 2:50) and an instruction form
rubric.partial: Keeps the time but not the instruction form

alternatives: At stage 2 both 'be there by 3:00' and 'the lesson starts at 3:00' fit; both options b and c are reasonable.
Students who answer 'ask the teacher' show good judgement.
hardCases: Does 10분 전까지 also allow arriving much earlier? Yes; 까지 sets a latest time.

cautions.language: 까지 sets a limit; 전 means before. 3시 10분 전 can be read as 2:50. -래요 reports an instruction, -ㄴ대요 a statement.
cautions.culture: Arriving early to class is a general expectation in many schools; nothing specific to Korea is required.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Times are given as words and numbers; screen readers read 2:50 differently, so it is written 3시 10분 전 in the Korean.

auto: Choices at each stage, checks of the repaired message

subject: korean
title: Same message, two listeners
goal: Pass one voice message on to two different listeners and choose which parts, what level of politeness and which reporting endings fit each listener.
thinking: Keeping the kind of message (request or news)
differsFromPlain: Plain practice turns one sentence into a report. Here one message goes to two listeners and the form, content and style must differ.
prerequisites: Can read short Korean messages with polite endings
Has seen 'someone told me ...' sentences in class
material:
민지 receives a voice message from 할머니:

'민지야, 할머니가 내일 병원에 가. 그래서 강아지 밥은 민우가 줘야 해. 그리고 네 아빠한테 저녁에 전화하라고 전해 줘.'

민지 (the older sister) must pass it on to 아빠 (polite style, respectful) and to her younger brother 민우 (casual style).

steps.prompt: Tell 아빠, in polite style, the part of the message that 아빠 needs.
selfAssess: Does my sentence let 아빠 know who asks and what to do?
Did I use respectful forms for 할머니 or 아빠?

modelAnswers.text: 할머니께서 저녁에 전화하시래요.
할머니께서 내일 병원에 가신대요. 저녁에 아빠한테 전화해 달라고 하셨어요.

badAnswers.why: Does not say who asked; not a report.
Gives different news and not the request.

steps.humanReview: Respectful forms (-시-, 께서) are optional here but show good control.
hints: Ask what 아빠 needs to do, and what he does not need to know.
Use 할머니께서 and a reporting ending that passes on a request.

steps.prompt: Now tell 민우 (casual style, no -요) what he has to do and why.
selfAssess: Is it clear that 민우 has to feed the dog?
Did I keep a casual style?

modelAnswers.text: 할머니가 내일 병원에 가신대. 그래서 네가 강아지 밥 주래.
할머니 내일 병원 가신대. 강아지 밥은 네가 주라고 하셨어.

badAnswers.text: 할머니가 병원에 가요. 강아지 밥 줘요.
badAnswers.why: Polite style and no reported form.
Does not say who asked; not a report.

steps.humanReview: Whether the message keeps its kind (request vs news) and fits the listener.
hints: Decide which part of the message is about 민우.
Casual style means no polite -요 ending.

rubric.full: Each version has the part that listener needs and no confusing extras
rubric.partial: One version has the wrong part

rubric.full: Polite for 아빠, casual for 민우, with reported endings
rubric.partial: Style or reporting ending is wrong in one

alternatives: For 민우, 네가 강아지 밥 주래 and 강아지 밥 주라고 하셨어 are both fine.
Adding why (병원) is optional but helps 민우.
hardCases: Whether the honorific -시- on 가신대 is natural in casual speech with a younger sibling: yes, for 할머니.

cautions.language: Reported speech changes 줘야 해 into 주래. Casual style has no -요, so -래요 becomes -래.
cautions.culture: Using respectful forms for grandparents is a core part of Korean family speech; students from other cultures may need this noted.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The two listeners are named in the instructions.

auto: Checks for names, content, reported form and style in each version

subject: korean
title: One relay keeps the reason
goal: Judge which relay keeps the real relationship between the facts of a note, then pass a contrast on with the right connector.
thinking: Reading how facts relate (reason, contrast, condition)
differsFromPlain: Plain practice fills a blank with -아서 or -지만. Here you test whether a relay keeps the same relationship as the original.
prerequisites: Can read short Korean notes
Has seen connectors such as -니까, -지만, -(으)면 and -는데 in class
material:
The teacher's note:

'내일은 현장학습이에요. 버스가 8시에 떠나요. 늦으면 기다릴 수 없어요. 그러니까 7시 50분까지 오세요.'

Four students each pass on the note to a friend who asks 'Why must I come by 7:50?'

steps.prompt: Which relay keeps the relationship between the facts?

options.reveals: 지만 joins facts that clash; the note has no clash.
You matched 그러니까 to a reason connector and kept the background fact.
-아도 says 'even if'; the note gives a reason, not a concession.
-면 comes from 늦으면 in the note but is attached to the wrong fact.

steps.explain: The note says: field trip (background), bus leaves at 8 (reason), so come by 7:50. Option b keeps that reason with -니까. The others change the relation to contrast (a), concession (c) or condition (d).
hints: Find the word that signals the reason in the note.
For each relay, say in English what relation its connector shows.

steps.prompt: Now the father says: '비가 와요. 그래도 우리는 캠핑을 가요.' Pass it on in one Korean sentence that keeps the contrast.
selfAssess: Does my sentence say that camping goes on although it rains?
Could my connector be read as a cause (because)?

modelAnswers.text: 아빠가 비가 오지만 캠핑을 간대요.
비가 와도 캠핑은 간다고 하셨어요.

badAnswers.why: 와서 shows a reason, so the meaning flips.
Loses the rain and is not a report.

steps.humanReview: Whether the connector fits naturally; -는데 can also show contrast.
hints: Decide which connector shows 'although' or 'even if'.
End with a form for reported statements.

rubric.full: Chooses b and can say what relation each connector shows
rubric.none: Chooses an option that changes the relation

rubric.full: Contrast connector plus a reported statement

alternatives: A student may also accept 비가 오는데 캠핑을 간대요 for contrast; it is natural.
Both 지만 and -아도 are valid for the contrast.
hardCases: The note's 늦으면 (condition) is not part of the relay in option b; leaving it out is fine.

cautions.language: -니까 (reason), -지만 (contrast), -아도 (even if), -(으)면 (condition) and -는데 (background) are all explained as relationships, not by translation word by word.
cautions.culture: School field trips are common worldwide; nothing special is assumed.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Option letters and Korean sentences are plain text.

subject: korean
title: Three kinds of message
goal: Invent a short teacher message made of three different kinds of sentences and pass it on with the matching endings.
thinking: Telling statements, requests and suggestions apart
Choosing the report ending that keeps the kind
differsFromPlain: Plain practice changes ready-made sentences. Here you make the message yourself and test your own report.
prerequisites: Can read short Korean messages with polite endings
Has seen 'someone told me ...' sentences in class
material: Imagine you are the class representative. The teacher gave the class some news, a request and an invitation to do something together. A friend who was absent asks you what the teacher said.

steps.prompt: Which report says that the teacher will also take part?

options.reveals: This reports a statement or plan, not an invitation.
You saw that 재요 passes on 'let's' and includes the teacher.
This reports an instruction to the class.

steps.explain: -재요 reports a suggestion 'let's ...' and includes the speaker. -래요 reports an instruction to the listeners, -ㄴ대요 reports a statement.
hints: Work backwards: for each report, say what the teacher's original sentence must have been.
Which original sentence would be said by someone who is going to clean too?

steps.prompt: Write 3 lines the teacher said (a fact, a request to the class, and a suggestion that includes the teacher), then write what you tell your friend, one reported sentence per line. Use one speech style, polite or casual, in all three reports.

checks.label: reports a request (not the copula 이래요)

selfAssess: Do my three original lines have three different kinds?
Does each reported line keep its kind?

modelAnswers.text:
선생님: 내일 시험이 없어요. 책을 가져오세요. 같이 청소해요.
전달: 선생님이 내일 시험이 없대요. 책을 가져오래요. 같이 청소하재요.

선생님: 오늘 숙제가 많아요. 내일까지 내세요. 우리 같이 도서관에 가요.
전달: 선생님이 숙제가 많대요. 내일까지 내래요. 같이 도서관에 가재요.

선생님: 시험이 끝났어요. 숙제를 내세요. 같이 점심 먹어요.
전달: 시험이 끝났대. 숙제를 내라고 하셨어. 같이 점심 먹자고 하셨어.

badAnswers.text: 선생님이 시험이 없대요. 책을 가져온대요. 청소한대요.
badAnswers.why: Only statement endings; requests and suggestions are lost.
Only one kind.
이래요 comes from the copula 이다 (a statement), not a request, and there is no suggestion.

steps.humanReview: Whether the three original lines really are different kinds and whether the reports match them.
hints: Pick any topic, but make the three kinds different.
Use a different ending for each kind when you report.

rubric.full: Three clearly different kinds of lines
Each report keeps the kind of its line

alternatives: Questions can be added as a fourth line with -냬요; not required here.
A student may use -다고 했어요 forms instead of -대요.
hardCases: Statements about a person (선생님이 학생이래요) look like -래요 but come from 이다 and are not a request.

cautions.language: -ㄴ/는대요 reports a statement, -(으)래요 an instruction, -자고 해요 (-재요) a suggestion; they are written without a space.
cautions.culture: Classroom talk about cleaning or homework is typical of Korean schools and is only an example.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The three forms are listed in the first step.

subject: korean
title: What the cousins need to know
goal: Read a phone conversation, decide which decisions the cousins need, and write a short message that says who decided what.
thinking: Writing a relay for a new audience
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reports one sentence at a time. Here you compress a longer conversation for a group who were not there.
prerequisites: Can read short Korean dialogues
Has seen 'someone told me ...' sentences in class
material:
은솔 overhears a phone call between 이모 and her mother:

이모: '언니, 할머니 생신 모임은 이번 토요일에 하자. 장소는 우리 집이 어때?'
엄마: '좋아. 그런데 아빠가 토요일 2시까지 일해. 저녁에 하면 어때?'
이모: '그래, 6시에 우리 집에서 보자. 케이크는 언니가 사 와.'
엄마: '알았어.'

Then 엄마 says to 은솔: '사촌들한테 할머니께 쓸 편지를 한 장씩 써 오라고 전해.' 은솔 will write in the cousins' group chat.

steps.prompt: What do the cousins need in the group chat? Choose all that they need to know or do.

options.reveals: You picked the decision that tells everyone when to come.
This was the reason for the time and not a decision the cousins must act on.
You picked the decision that tells everyone where to go.
Useful to know, but the cousins do not have to do anything about it.
You picked the task that is for the cousins.

acceptable.reason: The cake is a decision made in the call; adding it is fine as news.

steps.explain: The cousins need the time, the place and their own task (a letter). The reason for the time (아빠 works until 2:00) is only background; the cake is optional news.
hints: Mark each piece as a decision (agreed), a reason, or a task for the cousins.
Ask which pieces change what the cousins will do.

steps.prompt: Write the group-chat message in Korean (casual style is fine). Say who decided the time and place, and what the cousins have to bring.
selfAssess: Would a cousin know when, where and what to bring?
Did I say it was 엄마 and 이모 who decided?

modelAnswers.text: 엄마랑 이모가 토요일 6시에 이모네 집에서 보재. 할머니께 쓸 편지도 한 장씩 써 오래.
이모 집에서 토요일 저녁 6시에 모인대. 엄마가 편지를 한 장씩 써 오라고 했어.

badAnswers.why: No time or place; not a report; no source.
Time and place missing.

steps.humanReview: Whether the text is short and clear, and whether it separates decided plans from background.
hints: Name who decided (엄마 and 이모) and use a reporting ending.
Include the time, the place and the letter.

rubric.full: Chooses time, place and task and leaves out background
rubric.partial: Includes background or leaves out one decision

rubric.full: Gives source, time, place, letter with reported forms

alternatives: Adding the cake is acceptable.
Students may mention the day (토요일); it is useful.
hardCases: Is 'let's meet at 6' (보자) a decision or a suggestion? It was agreed by both, so reporting it as a plan is fine.

cautions.language: 보자 (let's meet) is reported as 보재; 써 오라고 해 is reported as 써 오래. Group chats often drop the polite -요.
cautions.culture: Family birthday gatherings with cousins are common; the example is not tied to a religion or region.
cautions.accessibility: No images. The dialogue is plain text with speaker names.

subject: korean
title: Where did the telephone game go wrong?
goal: Follow a message through four people, find the first link where its meaning changes, name the change, and repair it.
thinking: Comparing each link with the original
Naming what kind of change happened
differsFromPlain: Plain practice reports one message once. Here the message moves through several people and you find the first link where it changed.
prerequisites: Can read short Korean messages
Has seen 'someone told me ...' sentences in class
material:
선생님 said to the class:

'내일 1교시에 우리 반은 도서관에 가요. 도서관 카드는 꼭 가져오세요.'

The message was then passed on person to person:

steps.prompt: Which link is the first one where the meaning changes?
lines: 반장이 하나에게: 선생님이 내일 1교시에 우리 반이 도서관에 간대. 도서관 카드는 꼭 가져오래.
하나가 두리에게: 선생님이 내일 1교시에 우리 반이 도서관에 간다고 했어. 도서관 카드는 꼭 가져오라고 했어.
두리가 우진에게: 선생님이 내일 1교시에 우리 반이 도서관에 간대. 도서관 카드는 꼭 가져온대.
우진이 소라에게: 선생님이 내일 도서관 카드를 가져온대. 1교시는 도서관에서 한대.
steps.explain: Line 3 is the first change: 가져오세요 (an instruction) became 가져온대 (a statement), so it no longer says that the class must bring the card. Lines 1 and 2 keep it as an instruction. Line 4 repeats and adds more changes.
hints: Compare the card sentence of each line with the teacher's sentence.
Read only the ending of each card sentence: is it still an instruction?

steps.prompt: What exactly changed in the line you chose?

options.text: The time moved from tomorrow to today.
options.reveals: The word 내일 is still there in line 3.

options.text: The place changed from the library to a classroom.
options.reveals: 도서관 is in line 3 and unchanged.

options.text: The speaker changed from 선생님 to 하나.
options.reveals: Line 3 still says 선생님.

options.text: An instruction became news, so it is unclear who brings the card.
options.reveals: You looked at the ending and saw what type of message it reports.

steps.explain: Everything is the same except the card sentence: 가져오래 reports an instruction, 가져온대 reports a fact (as if someone is bringing a card).
hints: Compare line 3 with line 2 word by word and list the differences.
Which differences change who must do something?

steps.prompt: Write line 3 again so it passes on the teacher's message correctly (casual style).

checks.label: reports the card sentence as an instruction
does not report it as a statement

selfAssess: Does my sentence say that the class must bring the card?
Did I keep the time and place?

modelAnswers.text: 선생님이 내일 1교시에 우리 반이 도서관에 간대. 도서관 카드는 꼭 가져오래.
선생님이 내일 1교시에 우리 반이 도서관에 간다고 하셨어. 도서관 카드는 꼭 가져오라고 하셨어.

badAnswers.text: 선생님이 내일 1교시에 우리 반이 도서관에 간대. 도서관 카드는 꼭 가져온대.
badAnswers.why: Still reports a statement.
Not a report and loses the source.

steps.humanReview: Whether the rest of the line (time, place) is kept.
hints: Start with the part that is already right.
Change only the ending that reports the card sentence.

rubric.full: Picks line 3 and names the change
Instruction form, source and time/place kept

alternatives: Some students will say line 4 is the worst; step 1 asks for the first change.
A student who writes 가져오라고 하셨어 uses honorific for 선생님: good.
hardCases: Line 2 uses 간다고 했어 instead of 간대; both are correct forms and not a change.

cautions.language: -래 is the casual short form of -라고 해; the casual forms drop -요. -ㄴ대 and -라고 해 are different report types.
cautions.culture: Telephone games are common in many countries; no special background needed.
cautions.accessibility: No images. Lines are numbered 1 to 4 by the page, and each line names the two people involved.
